sections.title: Formations and tactics for the bots
sections.summary: Fifteen new scripted bot styles. Formations (wedge, line, echelon, finger four) and team tactics (false gap, pincer, hammer and anvil, Cantabrian circle, Lufbery circle, feigned retreat) give each ship a slot in a shape centred on its team, facing the control zone and then the enemy. Fighting pairs (a plain wingman pair and the Thach weave) split the team into leader-wingman pairs. Dogfight manoeuvres (break turn, flat scissors, skid) add a defensive move to the default bot whenever an enemy is on its tail. Every formation and team tactic beats the default bots (72 to 98%), and the pairs break even. The dogfight manoeuvres don't help (32 to 48%): ships turn a full circle in 1.5 s and can spin round to shoot while sliding, so nobody stays on a tail long enough for them to matter. The arena is small, so the shapes show mostly on the approach and when a team regroups.

sections.title: First GPU run: an attention population on Colab
sections.summary: Six attention-model teams, all copies of the attention model with three reward personalities, plus one exploiter, trained for 12 rounds on a Colab L4 GPU (about 70 minutes, 400k samples per member per round). The 'evolved' line took over, and its best member, m08, whose network grew to 384 units, led the last three rounds. On the gauntlet it scored 95%, against 91% for the attention model it started from, with the biggest gains against m16 (85% vs 70%) and the league striker (98% vs 90%). Head to head over 100 fresh battles it beat the attention model 66% of the time, though by a small average margin (+1.7 points per battle).

charts.alt: Elo of each population member by round over 12 rounds. The evolved members end on top; m08 leads the last three rounds at about 1,550, while the unchanged starting model sits between 1,260 and 1,440.

Gauntlet win rates with 95% intervals for five teams. Colab population best (m08): 98% vs bots, 92% vs rusher, 100% vs sniper, 98% vs zone, 98% vs league striker, 85% vs m16. Attention model: 95, 95, 100, 98, 90 and 70%. Population v2 best: 92, 90, 100, 88, 98 and 50%. MLP twin: 82, 90, 100, 92, 98 and 57%. m16: 82, 75, 100, 82 and 90%.

sections.title: Smarter: attention over entities
sections.summary: An attention network treats every ship, bullet and asteroid it can see as a separate item, and one transformer layer lets it weigh them against each other. The plain network (MLP) reads them as one long list of numbers. The attention model started as a copy of m16: it imitated m16's decisions over 200 battles, including two rounds where it flew and m16 marked what it should have done, and then won 40% against m16. Next, it and an MLP copy of m16 trained side by side for 8 rounds with identical settings. Both used a critic that sees the whole battle, opponents picked more often the more they win, and the three bot styles. On fresh battles the attention model beat its MLP twin 62% of the time (180 battles, rounds 6 to 8), and it scored 91% on the gauntlet, against 87% for the MLP and 86% for m16. Its biggest gains were against the rusher and zone bots, m16's weak spots. The cost: on 4 CPU cores it trains about 4 times slower (1,200 vs 4,800 samples per second).

charts.alt: Gauntlet win rates with 95% intervals for five teams. Colab population best (m08): 98% vs bots, 92% vs rusher, 100% vs sniper, 98% vs zone, 98% vs league striker, 85% vs m16. Attention model: 95, 95, 100, 98, 90 and 70%. Population v2 best: 92, 90, 100, 88, 98 and 50%. MLP twin: 82, 90, 100, 92, 98 and 57%. m16: 82, 75, 100, 82 and 90%.

sections.title: Population v2: better training, same network
sections.summary: Ten team models, all starting from m16 with three reward personalities (evolved, pack, guardian), trained with every upgrade. A critic that sees the whole battle; opponents chosen more often the more they win, including the three bot styles; two exploiters that train only to beat the current leader; and selection that never removes a line's last member. The run stopped after 8 of 16 planned rounds (about 2.5 hours on 4 cores) to free the CPU. An exploiter found a weakness once, at round 4, beating the leader 65% of the time. Line protection kept the guardian line alive in one slot. The gain was small. The best members rated 50 to 100 Elo above the unchanged m16 in their own tournaments. But on fresh battles the best, m17, scored 86% on the gauntlet, the same as m16: it beat the bots (92% vs 82%) and the rusher (90% vs 75%) more often, yet only broke even against m16 itself. With the same number of training samples per model, the attention model reached 91%, so for these MLP models the network, not the training method, now looks like the limit.

charts.alt: Population v2 Elo over 8 rounds with bots at 1000: the best member rises from about 1250 to 1357 at round 5 and ends at 1258; the median moves between about 1170 and 1290; the unchanged starting model stays between about 1200 and 1260. One exploiter success, at round 4.
Lineage of the 10 slots over 8 rounds: the evolved line grows from 4 to 6 slots, the pack line keeps 3, and the guardian line keeps 1 protected slot.

sections.title: An evolving population of teams
sections.summary: Population-based training: 8 team models, each with a genome (reward weights, learning rate, exploration, network width), seeded from the three league finalists. Every 2 rounds the bottom quarter was replaced by mutated copies of the top quarter, and a copy could grow its network by 64 units per layer without changing its play. In 16 rounds (about 3 hours on 4 CPU cores) the guardian line died out by round 2 and pack by round 6; striker descendants took over and kept improving. The winner, m16 (four generations from the striker, grown to 320 units), beat the bots in 77% (± 5%) of 60 fresh battles and the league striker in 87%. Its genome evolved to value kills (2.3 vs 1.5) and winning (3.75 vs 3.0) more, with a slower learning rate. Half the final population had grown networks (320 to 384 units); bigger nets were often but not always selected.

charts.alt: Population Elo over 16 rounds with bots at 1000: the median member rises from about 660 to 1260 and the best from about 1000 to 1311-1349; network width rises from 256 to a mean of 312 and a maximum of 384 units.
Lineage of the 8 population slots over 16 rounds: guardian descendants disappear after round 2, pack after round 6, and every slot ends as a striker descendant.

sections.title: Teams of agents vs teams of agents
sections.summary: Three team models with different reward personalities (striker: kills first; guardian: survival first; pack: fully shared team rewards and the zone) trained against each other, past snapshots and the bots for 12 rounds, about 1.5 hours on 4 CPU cores, under the competitive rules: control zone with reinforcements, weapon heat, 20 respawns, friendly fire, 384 px guns. All three started from the champion team model, which the bots beat 98% of the time under these rules: its spray-and-camp style kept its guns overheated 46% of the time. After an overheat penalty was added at round 4, the striker broke away and finished level with the bots. On 60 fresh battles it won 42% (± 6%) against the bots and 87% against the starting champion.

charts.alt: Elo per league member over 12 rounds with the bots fixed at 1000: the striker climbs from about 700 to 988; pack and guardian hover around the starting champion's 500 to 700.
Round 12 win rates: bots and striker are even (48/52%); both beat pack, the champion and the guardian 85 to 98% of the time; pack and the champion are even; the guardian loses to everyone.

sections.title: A trained team beats the bot team (classic rules)
sections.summary: One shared PPO policy flies all five blue ships against the built-in bots, each ship getting half of its teammates' kill and death rewards. Starting from the single-seat agent, it won 90% of battles after 2M ship-steps and every evaluation battle from 3M on (about 35 minutes on 4 CPU cores). Checked on 50 battles it had never seen, the 3M model still won 98%.

chart.alt: Team training progress: blue's win rate climbs from 45% to 100% and its average kill margin from -0.8 to +18.8 over 4M ship-steps; the all-bot team sits at 50% and -0.8.

sections.title: One trained agent among bots (classic rules)
sections.summary: A PPO agent flies blue ship 0; the other nine ships are the built-in bot. After 3.5M training steps it beats the bot playing the same seat, on 50 battles it never trained on. On its own it doesn't help a whole team: five copies win about as often as five bots, which is why the team training above was needed.
